description: Only these explicitly documented source/reply connections may drive primary recommended comparison. Keyword-based selection prohibited.

giver.question: Who confers a natural substantial form?
giver.scope: Differentiate the reported physical theory, Avicenna's rejection, material preparation, form-bestowal, and the later identification of the tenth intellect.

sequence.claim: A friction-only account wrongly presupposes corporeality without specific form.
sequence.why: Read the reported opponent and ensuing refutation in IX.5, rather than a sentence about the Active Intellect alone.

sequence.claim: Lāhījī first cites Avicenna's report of unnamed natural philosophers.
sequence.why: Section V starts with the mistaken physical account; it is not Lāhījī's settled doctrine.

sequence.claim: Lāhījī retells Avicenna's hylomorphic objection and form-bestowing explanation.
sequence.why: The reply answers the precise rival account just reported.

sequence.claim: The discussion then explains mixtures and dispositions leading to composite forms.
sequence.why: The next section requires this immediately preceding explanation.

sequence.claim: Section VI argues that the tenth intellect supplies rational souls and species forms.
sequence.why: The conclusion follows the discussion of preparation, not from a keyword match.

sequence.claim: Aquinas distinguishes generation of the form in matter from an abiding existential cause.
sequence.why: This is a later editorial comparison, not Aquinas answering Lāhījī historically.

links.explanation: Gawhar V explicitly retells Avicenna's Ilāhiyyāt IX.5, including the rejected friction hypothesis.
After establishing form-bestowal and physical dispositions, Gawhar VI asks which intellect is the source.
Both discuss formal production versus ongoing existence, but not with identical allocations.

dependence.question: Why does a contingent existent need an abiding cause?
dependence.scope: The thing's existential need is distinct from an artisan's time-limited preparation.

sequence.claim: VI.1 argues existence, not past temporal nonexistence, is the object of causal giving.
sequence.why: Use the whole closing proof rather than the isolated builder illustration.

sequence.claim: VI.2 resolves father, builder and fire, and separates simultaneous essential from successive preparatory causes.
sequence.why: The chapter directly follows VI.1 and depends on its demonstration.

sequence.claim: Lāhījī distinguishes potter or builder from conserving existential cause.
sequence.why: Similar thesis; no direct borrowing demonstrated.

sequence.claim: Aquinas distinguishes causation secundum fieri from secundum esse.
sequence.why: He independently addresses a closely parallel problem.

sequence.claim: Aquinas permits some secondary conservation under the First.
sequence.why: Avoid the false contrast that Aquinas rejects every intermediate conserving cause.

links.explanation: The second book VI chapter answers counterexamples to the first chapter's proof.
Lāhījī independently presents the continuing-need reasoning.
Both link conservation to caused esse but differ in other claims.

one.question: How can the absolutely One explain many effects?
one.status: direct continuous Persian argument partly restored
one.scope: Read all of Gawhar IV, including the ten-intellect qualification and the counterargument about fixed stars.

sequence.claim: Only one effect directly proceeds from the absolutely One.
sequence.why: This is Lāhījī reporting a philosophical rule, not a generic statement about all forms.

sequence.claim: Non-self-subsistent respects of the first intellect explain mediated plurality.
sequence.why: The response does not posit many independent effects directly from the First.

sequence.claim: Ten is not a proved upper limit; Ṭūsī's reading of the Ishārāt is cited.
sequence.why: This page was omitted in the old extraction.

sequence.claim: Lāhījī enumerates twelve possible third-level effects to answer Suhrawardī's fixed-star objection.
sequence.why: The opponent's objection, and the scope of the numerical reply, must both be shown.

sequence.claim: The objection is judged answered; Section V then shifts to elements.
sequence.why: Do not present the closing line as an unrelated claim about star counts.

links.explanation: The omitted pp.294–297 complete Section IV of Gawhar.
The following Section V tests form bestowal against elemental generation.

temporal.question: Why does this event arise now from an eternal cause?
temporal.scope: Distinguish universal causal dependence from the extra determination of the time of a novel effect.

sequence.claim: Successive preparatory conditions do not form a simultaneous essential regress.
sequence.why: This is in the complete VI.2 response, not an isolated formula.

sequence.claim: Contingency grounds need for being; temporal origination requires a further time-specific explanation.
sequence.why: This distinction follows Gawhar VI on form-bestowing intellect.

sequence.claim: Motion varies continuously, differentiating a cause's relation to an effect.
sequence.why: The earlier eternal principle is not altered by the new event.

sequence.claim: Material readiness reaches completion and the event receives existence.
sequence.why: This paragraph supplies the actual answer to why now.

links.explanation: Later formulation solves the same dependency-versus-temporal-novelty problem under a celestial hypothesis.
The intellect source was specified in Section VI; the timing of its effects is Section VII.

choice.question: Does necessity through willing negate genuine choice?
choice.status: reported objections, not direct multi-author collations
choice.scope: The question is the modal meaning of power when a complete cause includes will; it is not identical to whether natural causes exist.

sequence.claim: Extrinsic preference is insufficient until it becomes causally decisive.
sequence.why: Not in itself an account of voluntary alternative possibilities.

sequence.claim: An effect may be possible through itself but necessary with will as part of its completed cause.
sequence.why: Qūshjī is not directly edited here.

sequence.claim: If divine will is identical with essence, the modal possibility of not willing remains disputed.
sequence.why: The objection is a reported voice inside Astarābādī.

sequence.claim: A later response invokes newly arising choice or time-specific object of will.
sequence.why: Must not be attributed wholesale to the original Ṭūsī.

sequence.claim: Does benefiting others constitute a perfection gained by God?
sequence.why: This is a different question about riḍā/qaṣd, not a direct reply to Khafrī.

sequence.claim: God may withhold being through free willing.
sequence.why: Contrast rather than historical response.

links.explanation: The modal power dispute and the divine-purpose dispute have overlapping terms but different immediate questions.
Aquinas' free willing is a separate text and thesis, not a post-Tajrīd gloss.

making.question: What does the producer actually make—quiddity or actual being?
making.status: two different formulations and different source genres
making.scope: Separate a lexical report of simple/compound jaʿl from an independent treatment of particular existence.

sequence.claim: Simple making versus making a thing be something.
sequence.why: Lexicographic entry, not authorial Mīr Zāhid proof.

sequence.claim: Tahānawī quotes or reports Mīr Zāhid's gloss.
sequence.why: A nested report counts as one direct later witness.

sequence.claim: Debate over the production of quiddity and the relation of existence.
sequence.why: One must retain arguments and counterarguments together.

sequence.claim: Quiddity/existence attribution is mental, actual being not two self-subsisting things.
sequence.why: Narāqī is not directly replying to Tahānawī in this text.

sequence.claim: Longer Jawl debate can be reconstructed from Shawāriq.
sequence.why: This analytical chapter is not itself a new primary witness.

links.explanation: Both consider the object of making, but no documented exchange is established.

mind.question: Does apprehending heat make the mind hot?
mind.scope: The subject is mental representation, not a physical theory that a thought is the same as a hot body.

sequence.claim: Physical qualities and vast celestial magnitudes cannot be in the mind in the external sense.
sequence.why: Need to read the objections as directed against mental existence.

sequence.claim: Mental forms do not produce external physical concomitants.
sequence.why: Do not infer an unqualified metaphysical category of all mental objects.

sequence.claim: A related blackness/whiteness and mountain objection appears.
sequence.why: Different speakers must remain distinct in the composite witness.

sequence.claim: Actual external huwiyya differs from mentally represented quiddity.
sequence.why: Unsigned glosses must remain unsigned.

sequence.claim: Second intentions presuppose intelligibles qua intelligible.
sequence.why: Not a direct response to physical heat objection.

links.explanation: These two sources handle variants of the same classical objection with distinct apparatus.
Second-intention categorization is background rather than the exact objection.

motion.question: What actually changes in natural and substantial transformation?
motion.status: sources do not establish single continuous historical controversy
motion.scope: Separate substantial motion from alteration, generation and physical heat; do not use an Indian experiment as proof of Ṣadrian substantial motion.

sequence.claim: Matter cannot exist first as bare corporeality and later acquire all specific form.
sequence.why: The reply addresses a theory of elemental formation, not Ṣadrā's later continuous substance motion.

sequence.claim: Rehearses the critique of friction-only generation.
sequence.why: A distinct text on physical generation.

sequence.role: Editorial account of substantial motion debate
sequence.claim: Lāhījī's persistence objection and Ṣadrā's answer are surveyed.
sequence.why: Not a direct newly collated full Persian/Arabic exchange.

sequence.claim: Frictional heating and concealed fire concern natural alteration and generation.
sequence.why: This does not directly prove or refute the continuous substantial motion thesis.

links.explanation: Lāhījī reports Avicenna IX.5 with a direct source reference.
The material-change discussion is a different problem from Ṣadrā's substantial motion.

concept.question: Are existence and essence two external entities?
concept.status: two different primary considerations and editorial synthesis
concept.scope: Distinguish identity of a particular actuality from mental concept distinction and Thomist essence–esse composition.

sequence.claim: Predicative 'quiddity exists' need not posit two separate external objects.
sequence.why: The objection is directly about how the attribution is understood.

sequence.claim: Limitation grounds abstractable quiddity in contingent existence.
sequence.why: The intervening pages 73–81 are missing and must not be bridged.

sequence.claim: Externally united, mentally different respects are used in the procession proof.
sequence.why: This is not Narāqī answering an earlier author.

sequence.claim: Mental existence and essence predication form a wider philosophical problem.
sequence.why: Not another direct primary author.

links.explanation: Two later Persian authors deploy a similar distinction in different questions; no direct answer is shown.

created.question: Can the First Cause cease conserving what exists?
created.status: Thomist bounded question plus later Persian comparison
created.scope: Differentiate continuous dependence from divine freedom, possibility of withholding and actual annihilation.

sequence.claim: Creatures cannot sustain themselves independently of the First.
sequence.why: This is not yet a proof that God might choose to cease conserving.

sequence.claim: Created causes may participate subordinately in conserving effects.
sequence.why: Do not contrast Aquinas and Avicenna as pure intermediary/no intermediary.

sequence.claim: The source of created existence is free divine willing.
sequence.why: The possibility of cessation is a new modal claim.

sequence.claim: Aquinas denies that anything actually is annihilated.
sequence.why: Distinguish possible from actual.

sequence.claim: Riḍā/qaṣd controversy does not settle Aquinas' alternative possibilities.
sequence.why: Not an answer to Aquinas historically.

links.explanation: Articles 1–2 establish conservation; 3–4 then separate possibility of annihilation from its actuality.
Different authors address aspects of divine agency but no direct dialogue is claimed.
